docs.title: Welcome to the GurrLab
docs.text:
Oregon State University · Hatfield Marine Science Center · Newport, Oregon

This guide is your starting point for life in the GurrLab. It covers everything from lab culture and expectations to computing workflows, physical spaces, and role-specific onboarding paths.

This guide is iterative and input from colleagues and lab members is expected to strengthen the lab mission. Feedback is welcome at samuel.gurr@oregonstate.edu.

docs.text:
Use the tabs at the top to navigate between sections:

docs.title: Computing
docs.text:
The lab's computing stack is built around reproducibility and openness. Everything we produce: code, data, and analyses, lives in version control from day one.

Section Open Science Pre-registration, public code, data archiving Linux & Bash Navigation, file management, scripting Git & GitHub Version control and collaboration R & RStudio Statistical analysis and visualization HPC Cluster Large-scale computation

docs.text: Tool Purpose Bash / Linux Navigation, file management, scripting, HPC job submission Git & GitHub Version control for all code and documentation R & RStudio Statistical analysis, visualization, bioinformatics HPC cluster Large-scale computation for genomics, environmental modeling Discord Lab communication; #computing-help for technical questions OSF Pre-registration, data archiving, supplementary materials

docs.title: Linux & Bash
docs.text:
The command line gives you direct, scriptable control over your files, data, and compute jobs. Everything you do on the HPC will be in Bash.

Open a terminal:

  • macOS: Applications → Utilities → Terminal
  • Windows: Install Git Bash or use WSL
  • Linux: Already have one

docs.title: Navigating directories
docs.text:
pwd           # print working directory (where am I?)
ls            # list files in current directory
ls -lh        # list with details and human-readable sizes
ls -a         # include hidden files
cd Documents  # change into the Documents folder
cd ..         # go up one level
cd ~          # go to your home directory
cd -          # go back to the previous directory

docs.title: Reading & editing files
docs.text:
cat file.txt          # print entire file
head -20 file.txt     # first 20 lines
tail -20 file.txt     # last 20 lines
less file.txt         # scroll through (q to quit)
nano file.txt         # simple editor
vim file.txt          # powerful editor: press i to insert, Esc then :wq to save and quit

docs.title: Moving & copying
docs.text:
cp file.txt backup.txt          # copy file
cp -r folder/ folder_backup/    # copy a whole directory
mv file.txt new_name.txt        # rename
mv file.txt ../other_folder/    # move to another folder

docs.title: Deleting files
docs.text:
rm file.txt           # delete a file (permanent, no recycle bin)
rm -r folder/         # delete a folder and all contents

rm is permanent

There is no undo. Double-check before you run, especially with wildcards.

docs.title: Wildcards
docs.text:
ls *.csv              # list all .csv files
cp data_*.txt backup/ # copy all files matching the pattern

docs.title: Practice exercise
docs.text:
mkdir bash_practice
cd bash_practice
echo "Hello GurrLab" > hello.txt
cat hello.txt
cp hello.txt hello_copy.txt
ls -lh
rm hello_copy.txt
cd ..

docs.title: Git & GitHub
docs.text:
Git tracks changes to files so you can see history, revert mistakes, and collaborate without overwriting each other's work.

GitHub hosts Git repositories and adds collaboration features: pull requests, issues, and project boards.

docs.title: Setup & SSH
docs.text:
# Set your identity (do this once)
git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "you@oregonstate.edu"
git config --global core.editor "nano"

# Generate an SSH key
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "you@oregonstate.edu"

# Copy the public key
cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub
# Paste into GitHub → Settings → SSH and GPG keys → New SSH key

docs.title: Clone a repository
docs.text:
git clone git@github.com:GurrLab/your-repo.git
cd your-repo

docs.title: Daily workflow
docs.text:
git pull                              # get latest changes
# ... make your edits ...
git status                            # see what changed
git add analysis.R                    # stage a specific file
git add .                             # stage all changes
git commit -m "Add CO2 analysis"      # commit with a message
git push                              # push to GitHub

Good commit messages

Use the imperative mood: "Add...", "Fix...", "Update..." rather than "Added...". Be specific: "Fix salinity calibration in water_chem.R" not "fix bug".

docs.title: Branches & pull requests
docs.text:
git checkout -b feature/new-analysis   # create and switch to a new branch
# ... make changes ...
git add .
git commit -m "Add new analysis approach"
git push -u origin feature/new-analysis

Then on GitHub: open a Pull Request from your branch into main. Request a review. Merge after approval.

docs.title: Merge conflicts
docs.text:
<<<<<<< HEAD
result <- model_a(data)
=======
result <- model_b(data)
>>>>>>> feature/new-analysis

Edit the file to keep what you want, remove the markers, then:

git add conflicted_file.R
git commit -m "Resolve merge conflict"

docs.title: New repository checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] Create repo in the GurrLab GitHub org, not your personal account
  • [ ] Add a README.md describing the project and how to run the code
  • [ ] Add a .gitignore for your language (R, Python)
  • [ ] Make the repo public unless there is a specific reason not to
  • [ ] Never commit raw data files > 50 MB. Use OSF or the lab NAS instead.

docs.title: HPC Cluster
docs.text: The OSU HPC cluster is where you run large jobs: genome assembly, environmental modeling, permutation tests with thousands of iterations.

docs.title: Getting an account
docs.text: Request an account through [HPC documentation, link TBD]. Copy the PI on your request email.

docs.title: Connecting
docs.text: ssh your_onid@submit.hpc.oregonstate.edu

docs.title: Submitting a job (SLURM)
docs.text:
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=my_analysis
#SBATCH --output=logs/job_%j.out
#SBATCH --error=logs/job_%j.err
#SBATCH --time=04:00:00
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=8
#SBATCH --mem=32G
#SBATCH --mail-type=END,FAIL
#SBATCH --mail-user=you@oregonstate.edu

module load R/4.3.0
Rscript analysis.R

Submit: sbatch job.sh · Monitor: squeue -u your_onid

docs.title: Good HPC habits
docs.text:
• Test on a small dataset locally before submitting large jobs
  • Use --time conservatively and overestimate to avoid job termination
  • Clean up /scratch after jobs complete (scratch is not backed up)
  • Document your software versions with module list in your job output

docs.title: Open & Transparent Science
docs.text:
We pre-register study designs, share code and data publicly, and archive null results alongside positive ones. This isn't overhead. It is how we make our science trustworthy and durable.

  • Pre-registration: Register your study design on OSF before data collection. This protects against unconscious p-hacking and signals scientific integrity to reviewers.
  • Public code: All analysis code is published in the lab GitHub org at or before paper submission. Comment your code as if someone else will run it, because they will.
  • Data archiving: Raw data are archived in a domain repository (e.g., NCBI, BCO-DMO, OSF) at publication.
  • Null results: Experiments that don't go as planned are still science. Document and report them.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text:
Download and install in this order:

  1. R (the language)
  2. RStudio (the IDE)

Core packages to install:

install.packages(c(
  "tidyverse",   # data wrangling and visualization
  "here",        # reproducible file paths
  "rmarkdown",   # reproducible reports
  "devtools"     # installing packages from GitHub
))

docs.title: Reproducible project structure
docs.text:
Use RStudio Projects (.Rproj) for every analysis. Never use setwd().

my_project/
├── data/
│   ├── raw/          # never modify these
│   └── processed/
├── R/                # scripts and functions
├── output/
│   ├── figures/
│   └── tables/
├── docs/
└── README.md

Use here::here() for file paths:

library(here)
data <- read_csv(here("data", "raw", "samples.csv"))

docs.title: Code of Conduct
docs.text:
A psychologically safe and harassment-free working environment is pivotal to enable us to belong and be challenged together.

Harassment includes, but is not limited to, offensive verbal comments related to gender, gender identity and expression, age, sexual orientation, disability, socioeconomic status, physical appearance, body size, race, or religion; sexual images in public spaces; deliberate intimidation; stalking; harassing photography or recording; sustained disruption of events; inappropriate physical contact; and unwelcome sexual attention.

Lab members asked to stop any harassing behavior are expected to comply immediately.

docs.title: Reporting
docs.text:
If you are being harassed, notice that someone else is being harassed, or have any other concerns:

  • Talk to the PI directly. The door is always open.
  • OSU Office of Equal Opportunity and Access (EOA): 2150 SW Jefferson Way, 330 Snell Hall · 541-737-3556 · eoa.oregonstate.edu
  • Graduate ombudsperson: gradschool.oregonstate.edu. This is a confidential and neutral resource.
  • OSU Policies: policy.oregonstate.edu

docs.title: What You Can Expect From Me
docs.text: These are the PI's commitments to every lab member.

docs.title: Time and feedback
docs.text:
• Regular meetings: bi-weekly 1-on-1s at minimum, with more frequency during critical periods
  • Manuscript and proposal feedback returned within 2 weeks of submission
  • Response to emails and Discord messages within 2 business days under normal circumstances

docs.title: Mentorship and advocacy
docs.text:
• Strong letters of recommendation written with care and submitted on time
  • Introductions to collaborators and professional networks relevant to your work
  • Nomination for awards and fellowships as opportunities arise
  • Honest, constructive feedback about your progress, strengths, and areas for development

docs.title: Resources
docs.text:
• Funding for tuition, stipend, and research per OSU graduate student agreements
  • Support for conference attendance at least once per year when work is being presented
  • Clear authorship conversations early in every project, with no surprises at submission
  • A co-created IDP reviewed annually

docs.title: Lab climate
docs.text:
• A harassment-free, inclusive environment as described in the Code of Conduct
  • Transparency about lab finances, project status, and future directions where relevant
  • Openness to feedback about my own mentoring style and the lab's culture

docs.title: What I Expect From You
docs.text: These expectations apply to all lab members. They are meant to support your growth, not to micromanage it.

docs.title: Scientific integrity
docs.text:
• Be honest about your data and results. Report what you found, not what you hoped to find.
  • Document everything at time of collection. A lab notebook entry written a week later is a reconstruction.
  • Pre-register your study designs on OSF before data collection begins.
  • Archive all data and code publicly at or before publication. No exceptions.

docs.title: Communication
docs.text:
• Be proactive. If you are stuck, behind, or uncertain, say so early.
  • Honor your commitments. If you agreed to deliver something, deliver it. If circumstances change, communicate before the deadline, not after.
  • Respect your colleagues, mentors, and mentees. Expect to both give and receive productive critique.
  • Communicate schedule changes ≥ 48 hours in advance when possible, especially for husbandry responsibilities.

docs.title: Lab citizenship
docs.text:
• Attend lab meetings unless a scheduling conflict is communicated in advance.
  • Contribute to shared tasks: cleaning, stocking, and maintaining communal spaces.
  • Mentor junior members as you gain seniority. This is a professional obligation, not optional.
  • Treat all organisms with care. Hatfield has a resident veterinarian who conducts unannounced welfare checks.

docs.title: Your work
docs.text:
• Write every week. Even rough draft material. Writing is thinking.
  • Present your work at lab meeting annually at minimum.
  • Make your code and data open from the start. Version-control everything on GitHub.

🧪 FRA

Faculty Research Assistants are professional staff scientists who provide continuity, technical expertise, and institutional memory. The lab depends deeply on your skills and leadership in the lab space.

docs.title: Graduate Student
docs.text:
🎓 Graduate

Graduate students are the intellectual core of the lab. You are here to develop as an independent scientist, and the lab provides resources, mentorship, and community to support that journey.

docs.title: Onboarding timeline
docs.text:
Weeks 1–2: Arrive & orient

  • Complete all OSU + HMSC onboarding paperwork
  • Set up computing environment (SSH, GitHub, R, HPC account)
  • Read 10–15 foundational papers in your project area
  • Schedule a lab meeting intro presentation within 60 days

Months 1–3: Define your questions

  • Draft a 1–2 page research prospectus
  • Identify committee members (M.S.: 2 + PI; Ph.D.: 3 + PI)
  • Establish a regular meeting cadence with the PI
  • Begin preliminary data collection or literature synthesis

Year 1–2: Research & milestones

  • Pass qualifying / comprehensive exams per program requirements
  • Pre-register your study design on OSF before data collection
  • Present annually at lab meeting and/or an external conference
  • Submit a first manuscript draft within 18 months of data collection

Final year: Writing & defense

  • Three chapters minimum (Ph.D.) or two (M.S.) in manuscript format
  • Submit chapters to co-authors 4 weeks before submission deadline
  • Schedule dissertation defense ≥ 3 months in advance
  • Archive all data and code publicly before or at defense

docs.title: Expectations
docs.text:

  • Own your project. The PI mentors but you drive.
  • Write every week, even when it is rough draft material
  • Be a good lab citizen: mentor undergrads, contribute to lab tasks
  • Publish your work and make data/code openly available
  • Bi-weekly 1-on-1 meetings (or more during crunch periods)
  • Manuscript feedback returned within 2 weeks
  • Funding for tuition, stipend, and research per OSU agreement
  • Nomination and support for awards, fellowships, and conferences

docs.title: Postdoctoral Fellow
docs.text:
🔬 Postdoc

Postdoctoral fellows are independent scientists building toward a faculty or senior research position. The lab supports that goal. We collaborate closely and prioritize your career development.

docs.title: Onboarding timeline
docs.text:
Weeks 1–3: Systems & strategy

  • Complete all HR, benefits, and HMSC onboarding paperwork
  • Set up HPC account; clone all relevant lab repositories
  • Schedule a 2-hour onboarding meeting with PI to map a 2-year plan
  • Draft a brief IDP within 30 days

Months 1–6: Establish independence

  • Submit or revise first manuscript within 6 months
  • Identify 1–2 fellowship/grant opportunities to apply for
  • Present work at an external conference or seminar
  • Begin mentoring a graduate student or undergraduate

Year 1–2: Productivity & visibility

  • Maintain 2–3 active manuscripts at any time
  • Apply for ≥ 1 independent grant per funding cycle
  • Develop a teaching or outreach portfolio if targeting faculty roles
  • Draft a research statement and CV annually

docs.title: Undergraduate Student
docs.text:
📚 Undergraduate

Undergraduate researchers develop transferable skills in experimental design, data collection, and scientific communication while contributing to real ongoing research.

docs.title: Onboarding timeline
docs.text:
Weeks 1–2: Foundations

  • Complete HMSC lab safety training
  • Set up GitHub and join the GurrLab org
  • Schedule a 1-on-1 with the PI to define your semester goals
  • Read the Welcome and Computing sections

Weeks 3–6: Skill development

  • Work through the Bash tutorial
  • Complete the GitHub workflow exercise
  • Shadow a graduate student on data collection or processing

Weeks 7–12: Independent research

  • Maintain a lab notebook with methods and observations
  • Conduct assigned experiments or fieldwork
  • Prepare a short progress update (slides or summary document)

End of semester: Wrap-up

  • Archive data and code to the lab GitHub repository
  • Complete the lab exit/reflection form
  • Discuss next steps: continuation, thesis, or reference letter
  • Produce an open, citable output from your time in the lab (see below)

docs.title: Leaving something behind
docs.text:
A core expectation for undergraduate researchers is that your time in the lab produces something permanent, public, and citable: something you can point to in a CV, graduate school application, or job interview that shows you did real science.

This doesn't require a peer-reviewed paper. It does require intention. Talk with the PI during your final few weeks about which format fits your project. Options include:

Figshare: Upload a research poster, dataset, figure, or summary report. Figshare assigns a DOI, making your work permanently citable. This is a low-barrier way to get a citable item on your CV regardless of whether a full manuscript follows.

The Filter Feed: The GurrLab blog at gurr-lab.com. Write a short post (500–1000 words) summarizing your project, what you found, and what it means: written for a curious general audience rather than specialists. Posts are authored and attributed, giving you a public, shareable link to your work.

GitHub repository: if your project involved code or data analysis, a well-documented public repository with a README and a Zenodo-linked release is itself a citable, referenceable artifact.

Start early

The best outputs are drafted before your final week, not during it. Plan your wrap-up deliverable at the start of your last month and use the PI's feedback cycle to get it right.

docs.title: Poster presentation opportunities
docs.text:
Presenting a poster is one of the most effective ways to build confidence, practice scientific communication, and make your work visible to a broader community. The lab actively encourages undergraduate researchers to pursue at least one presentation opportunity during their time here. Talk to the PI early, as many of these have abstract deadlines weeks before the event.

HMSC Coastal Summer Research Symposium An annual symposium hosted at Hatfield Marine Science Center celebrating undergraduate and graduate research conducted at the coast. Open to all HMSC-affiliated researchers. An excellent first venue with a familiar setting, supportive audience, and a natural fit for GurrLab work. docs.title: Volunteer
docs.text:
🌱 Volunteer

Volunteers are the heartbeat of day-to-day lab operations. You will gain hands-on experience with marine science research while contributing directly to active projects.

docs.title: Onboarding timeline

Weeks 2–4: Shadowing & skill-building

  • Shadow a graduate student or FRA on a core lab task each week

Month 2+: Independent contribution

  • Take ownership of a defined task or sub-project
  • Maintain a lab notebook for all work
  • Attend and contribute to lab meetings
  • Discuss continued involvement and goals with the PI

docs.title: Lab Philosophy
docs.text:
Five interlocking pillars define how we work, mentor, and grow together. These aren't abstract ideals. They shape how we run meetings, give feedback, assign authorship, and support one another day to day.

Expected of all lab members

Reading and agreeing to this chapter is a condition of joining the lab, not a suggestion. If something here raises a question or concern, bring it to the PI. That conversation is welcome and expected.

# Pillar 1 Belong to be challenged 2 Reciprocal expectations 3 Structured skill development 4 Rigorous, ethical research practice 5 Continuous reflection & growth

docs.title: Belong to Be Challenged
docs.text:
The leader's first responsibility is to cultivate a psychologically healthy research environment where mentees can give, receive, and act on feedback without fear of personal attack, retaliation, or humiliation. This includes explicitly normalizing that everyone makes mistakes, treating lapses as opportunities to learn, and addressing uncivil or insensitive behavior through calm, non-defensive conversations that focus on patterns rather than isolated incidents.

A humanistic approach emphasizes respect and compassion for every lab member regardless of career stage, background, or role, recognizing that people bring diverse histories and tolerance levels for incivility to work. The mentor sets the tone by modeling dignity and respect in all interactions and by ensuring a safe and supportive environment free from harassment and discrimination, consistent with institutional policies and mandatory reporting obligations.

Psychological safety defined

"Psychological safety is defined as a shared belief that the team is safe for interpersonal risk-taking. Such interpersonal risks include open communication, voicing concerns, asking questions and seeking feedback without fear of judgment." — Hardie et al. (2022), BMC Medical Education

docs.title: Diverse perspectives make better science
docs.text:
Science is enriched, not just ethically but intellectually, by people who think differently. Lab members come to this work with different cultural backgrounds, educational histories, career trajectories, and ways of framing problems. Those differences are a resource. A question that seems naive from one vantage point may expose an assumption the rest of the group has been silently carrying for months.

We are therefore intentional about making space for a full range of voices in lab meetings, paper discussions, and experimental design. This means pushing back on the tendency to defer to seniority or confidence, and actively inviting perspectives from people who may be less likely to volunteer them. No one should feel that their background makes their contributions less credible here.

docs.title: Giving and receiving critique
docs.text:
Critical feedback is one of the most valuable things we give one another, and one of the hardest to do well. The goal of critique in this lab is not to identify flaws for their own sake, but to strengthen the work and develop the scientist.

When giving feedbackWhen receiving feedback

→ Be specific. Vague praise or vague criticism are both hard to act on. Name the sentence, the analysis step, the logical gap.

→ Critique the work, not the person. "This conclusion isn't supported by the data shown" lands differently than "you misread the data."

→ Pair problems with possibilities. If you flag an issue, try to suggest at least one direction forward, even if that direction is "I'm not sure, but it's worth exploring."

→ Consider the moment. A lab meeting mid-presentation and a one-on-one manuscript review call for different registers. Read the context.

→ Try to hear the critique before responding to it. Defensiveness is a natural first reflex. Let it pass before deciding how to reply.

→ Ask for specifics if you don't have them. "Can you say more about what you mean?" is always a reasonable response.

→ You don't have to agree. Feedback is data, not instruction. Consider it seriously, then use your own judgment to decide what to do with it.

→ Close the loop. When you've acted on feedback, say so. It signals that the exchange was worthwhile and encourages the reviewer to keep engaging.

A note on discomfort

Being challenged, having a hypothesis questioned or a draft returned heavily revised, can feel discouraging. That discomfort is not a sign that something has gone wrong. It is usually a sign that something is about to get better. The lab's job is to deliver challenge with care; your job is to meet it with openness.

docs.title: Rigorous, Ethical Research Practice
docs.text:
Responsible conduct is woven into routine lab life, not saved for a one-time training. This includes explicit instruction and ongoing discussion about scientific rigor: reproducibility, accurate record-keeping, appropriate statistics, data normalization, and outlier handling. It also covers authorship norms and appropriate credit based on material and intellectual contribution.

All lab members are expected to complete required RCR and safety trainings, understand ethical and regulatory expectations (human and animal subjects, biosafety, data confidentiality, conflicts of interest), and follow clear policies for data ownership, sharing, and handling during lab transitions.

Data ownership

The PI is custodian of all lab data. Raw data, analysis scripts, and lab notebooks remain with the lab when a member departs. Talk to the PI before your end date about archiving your work in the shared lab repositories.

docs.title: Reciprocal Expectations
docs.text:
Effective mentorship is framed as a mutual agreement with clearly articulated expectations in both directions, ideally documented in a living advisor–advisee agreement co-revised over time. The mentor specifies expectations around honesty, communication, lab presence, authorship discussion, and contribution to shared responsibilities, while also stating what trainees can reliably expect from the mentor: regular meetings, timely feedback, advocacy, networking support, and letters of recommendation.

Mentees are responsible for their own careers: actively seeking advice, critically evaluating it, and taking ownership of scientific direction within the broad themes of the lab, including raising concerns, setting boundaries, and considering lab changes if interests diverge.

In practice

This is why the expectations section of this guide is bidirectional: what the PI expects from you, and what you can expect from the PI. Both are commitments.

docs.title: Continuous Reflection & Growth
docs.text:
A central tenet is ongoing reflection and willingness to seek advice, adapt, and improve communication and leadership skills. The mentor regularly invites candid feedback about the lab climate and their own mentoring, treats criticism as valuable data, and when missteps occur, de-escalates, acknowledges impact, and works with mentees to decide how to move forward constructively.

Mentees are encouraged to self-assess strengths and areas for development, to signal when they need more structure or support, and to build a broader mentoring network beyond the primary PI.

Throughout, mentorship is a collaborative, evolving relationship in which mentor and mentees co-create a respectful, rigorous, and inclusive research community, one that supports both excellent science and sustainable, humane careers.

docs.title: Structured Skill Development
docs.text:
Mentorship encompasses systematic development of research, communication, and leadership skills across career stages. This means intentional training in study design, power analysis, lab notebook practice, sample management, solution preparation, and data management. SOPs and templates are used to scaffold good habits and reproducible work.

Professional development includes guiding course choices, conference participation, grant writing, and outreach, and encouraging mentees to pursue independent ideas that align with lab themes while learning to present those ideas through proposals and presentations.

A core expectation is that more senior mentees practice mentoring themselves, for example by supervising undergraduates, with the PI supporting this as both a training experience and a way to propagate healthy mentoring practices through the group.

docs.title: Lab Norms
docs.text:
These aren't rules so much as working agreements that let the lab function well.

  • Challenges and null results are worth sharing, often more so than positive ones. An experiment that found no effect, an approach that didn't pan out, or a method that failed under real conditions is exactly the kind of knowledge the lab community needs. Sharing these openly saves others from repeating dead ends, sharpens our collective thinking, and reflects the honest practice of science. No finding is too small or too "negative" to bring to the group.
  • Document at time of collection. A lab notebook entry written a week later is a reconstruction, not a record.
  • Ask early, not late. If you are stuck, confused, or behind, say so. The PI would far rather hear about a problem early than discover it at a deadline.
  • Clean up after yourself. Shared bench space, cold rooms, and husbandry areas depend on everyone.
  • Respect organism welfare. Your husbandry schedule deserves diligence and consistency. Hatfield has a resident veterinarian who conducts unannounced welfare checks. Neglect of organisms in any space, shared or otherwise, is not acceptable and will be addressed directly.

docs.title: A shared foundation
docs.text:
Day-to-day norms only hold when everyone understands the values behind them. The Lab Philosophy chapter articulates the five pillars that underpin how we work, mentor, give feedback, and grow together: psychological safety, reciprocal expectations, and rigorous ethical research practice.

Required reading and agreement

Every lab member is expected to read the Lab Philosophy chapter in full before or during their first week, and to signal to the PI that they have done so. This isn't a formality. The philosophy shapes decisions the lab makes every day: how critique is delivered, how authorship is discussed, how conflicts are resolved. Understanding it is a prerequisite for full participation in the lab community.

If anything in the philosophy chapter raises a question, concern, or point of disagreement, bring it to the PI. That conversation is exactly the kind the lab is designed to support.
